input.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's: if you are a domestic dog, a review reports an estimate of 20/75 for a typical dog, so you would have to stand 20 feet from what a human can make out from 75 feet. If you are a red fox, the cells in your retina allow about 6 cycles a degree, roughly a fifth of a human's 30. If you are an arctic fox, the estimate is about 9.
input.note: Left out coyotes, wolves, jackals and other foxes (carried grade g) to keep to three sentences; unmeasured species not named.

input.text: A light flashing 80 times a second looks steady to a human, who stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second. If you are a peregrine falcon, you see flicker at 125 flashes a second at least, if you are a saker falcon, at 100, and if you are a Harris's hawk, at 80. If you are a kestrel or another falcon of the genus Falco, you very likely see flicker at a fast rate like your relatives the peregrine and the saker, and for any other hawk, eagle or kite nobody has measured it.
input.note: Peregrine figure is a lower bound ("at least 129"), so I rounded down to 125. No numbers given for carried falcons.

input.text: If you are an American bullfrog, green frog, northern leopard frog, European common frog or European toad, your pupil is a horizontal almond-shaped slit, though a red-eyed treefrog's is vertical. If you are a northern leopard frog, you see about 3 cycles a degree, roughly a tenth of the 30 that a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is, and nobody has measured sharpness in most other frogs and toads.
input.note: No record gives a field of view for any frog or toad, so that part says so. The sharpness figure is kept to the northern leopard frog because numbers do not travel between species.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a heron, egret, crane or ibis, or how closely spaced the light-sensing cells in your eye are. The only birds in this group with a figure are two doves: a compilation reports that a rock pigeon reads about 12 cycles a degree in behavior tests, and a mourning dove about 7, estimated from cell counts in its retina. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree.
input.note: No record gives acuity or receptor spacing for any heron, egret, crane, coot or ibis, so the row stays at i and mentions only the pigeon and mourning dove figures.

input.text: A low tone played from more than 3 meters away makes a bold jumping spider freeze, and male brilliant jumping spiders court with vibrations whose rate affects how well they mate. Those are two of the few jumping spiders measured for sound or vibration. Nobody has measured what you hear or feel through your legs if you are any other jumping spider.
input.note: Left out R1 (recorded under Corythalia canosa, not matched to the listed name), R3 and R5 to stay within three sentences.

input.text: You have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. This has been measured in the domestic dog, the red fox and the arctic fox, and each has two kinds.
input.note: Left out wavelengths (429 and 555 nm) and any claim about which colors look gray, since no record states what dogs or foxes see as gray.

input.text: If you are a cane toad, a review reports that a light flashing faster than about 7 times a second looks steady to you, the lowest value in its table, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60. Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see if you are any other frog or toad, so nobody can say whether you are as slow as the cane toad.
input.note: Only the cane toad has a figure, read from a review table; I did not carry it to other Rhinella toads in the text.

input.text: Your eyes sit on the sides of your head, and a book on deer says they take in almost a complete circle, about 310 degrees. The book does not say how that was found, and nobody has measured how much of your view both eyes share. In goats, which are not deer, a review reports a field of 320 to 340 degrees, with 20 to 60 degrees shared by both eyes.
input.note: No deer record measures field or binocular overlap; R10 is a book statement with no stated method, so I attributed it to the book. Goat figures are named as goat figures only.

input.text: If you are a domestic dog with a long skull, as a wolf has, you see most sharply along a horizontal band level with the horizon, and if you have a short nose like a pug, you see most sharply in one spot in the middle. A red fox has a distinct spot plus a moderate band, and an Arctic fox has a distinct spot. Nobody has measured this in the other members of the dog family, so if you are a coyote, a jackal or another relative, nobody knows where your eyes see most sharply.
input.note: Left out the Arctic fox's streak and all cell-density numbers: the Arctic fox quote states only the spot, and the numbers had no comparison job.

input.text: If you are an American alligator, the dark opening in the middle of each eye is a vertical slit. If you are a China alligator, you very likely have the same, since your close relative the American alligator does. Among crocodiles only the saltwater crocodile has been measured, and it has a vertical slit that a report calls mobile, and nobody has measured the pupil shape of the other species.
input.note: Caiman, gharial and most crocodile species have no pupil record, so the row says nobody has measured them.

input.text: If you are a wood strawberry, you sense red and far-red light with a protein called phytochrome B, and a review reports that your daughter plants grow more root over a live patch than over a dead one. If you are a common selfheal, a review reports that strong far-red light slowed the growth of your plantlets in a lab. For most of you, nobody has measured whether you sense a neighbor by its light or by its scent.
input.note: Left out the dandelion: R1 only says it was tested as a receiver of neighbors' airborne volatiles, with no result stated. No record says neighbors change the light a plant gets, so I did not say that.

input.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's. In trained bees that had to tell stripes apart, the honeybee, the buff-tailed bumblebee and the common eastern bumblebee each saw about a hundredth as much fine detail as a human. For most other bees and wasps, nobody has measured how sharply they see.
input.note: Left out hornet, wasp and carpenter bee figures: they come from eye anatomy or partial tables, and the row grade is i.

input.text: Two of your relatives, the saltwater crocodile and the freshwater crocodile, have a streak of sharpest vision that runs across the back of each eye from the nose side to the temple side. At its best the saltwater crocodile sees about 9 cycles a degree, less than a third of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured where your sharpest spot lies or how sharply you see.
input.note: Records cover only Crocodylus species; nothing for Alligator, so the row stays at i.

input.text: In every jumping spider measured, the big front eyes have cells that sense ultraviolet and cells that sense green. A regal jumping spider has three kinds of color-sensing cell, and Habronattus pyrrithrix gets a third color channel, for red, only in a small patch at the center of the retina, while Plexippus validus has just two kinds. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have unless you are one of those species.
input.note: Left out the color-discrimination behavior (R12, Evarcha falcata) and wavelength figures because they add no comparison here. R8 gives three cell types in the regal jumping spider but does not say which kinds, so the row does not say.

input.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In the monarch, the cabbage white, the small tortoiseshell, the drone fly, the seven-spotted ladybird beetle and the green darner dragonfly, one kind of color-sensing cell is most sensitive to ultraviolet, and you very likely have such a cell too.
input.note: Left out spectral-range claims: no record gives a range for most species here, and dragonflies have none.

input.text: Measurements in the honey bee, the buff-tailed bumblebee, the large red-tailed bumblebee and the European wool carder bee found three kinds of color-sensing cell, with peaks in ultraviolet, blue and green. None of them peaks in red, not even in the large red-tailed bumblebee. If you are one of these four, that is how your eyes are built, and if you are another bee, you very likely have the same three kinds.
input.note: No record says how red things look to a bee, so I left out the "look dark" claim from the example row.

input.text: If you are a black-crowned night heron, you see about 320 degrees around your head at once, and if you are a common moorhen, about 300 degrees, with a blind area directly behind you. Both of your eyes see the same thing only in a narrow, upright strip in front of you, about 20 degrees wide in the night heron and about 35 degrees wide in the moorhen. Nobody has measured how wide a field most other waders see, including the great blue heron.
input.note: Left out the pigeon and the cattle egret figures to keep the row short; the pigeon's 316 degrees comes from an unlabeled table column.

input.text: In jumping spiders tested with an eyetracker, the retinas inside the two big front eyes move, and they spend more time looking at still or slowly moving images. If you are a bold jumping spider, your front eyes need guidance from the smaller eyes beside them to find and track a moving object, but they scan a still shape just as well without it. Of the jumping spiders that borrow this view, only the bold jumping spider has had its eye movement measured, so nobody has measured how your own retinas move.
input.note: Left out the fovea: R5's quote does not state the receptor density figure, and R3 covers only Lyssomanes.

input.text: Your eyes very likely have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. In the Eurasian red squirrel, a relative in the same genus as the gray squirrel and the fox squirrel, one kind senses short, blue wavelengths and the other senses middle to long wavelengths. If you are an eastern gray squirrel, your two kinds peak at about 445 and 545 nanometers, and in the fox squirrel they peak at about 450 and 540.
input.note: Kept to the squirrel genus Sciurus; no record gives a human peak, so the numbers are not compared with a human's.

input.text: Your pupil is a slit lying on its side, wider than it is tall. It has been recorded this way in white-tailed deer, red deer, moose, reindeer (caribou), pudu and gray brocket. If you are a reindeer, the slit measures about 25 square millimeters when narrowed and opens into a round pupil about 13 times larger in area.
input.note: No record gives the pupil of mule deer, roe deer or fallow deer, so the row names only the measured deer.

input.text: A lamp that looks steady to a human can look like it is flashing to a European pied flycatcher, which sees flicker at up to about 145 flashes a second, where a human stops seeing it at about 60. A blue tit has been measured at about 130 flashes a second and an Anna's hummingbird at 70 to 80. For most other birds, nobody has measured how fast you see, so if you are not one of these three, your number is not known.
input.note: Left out the compiled values (starling, cowbird, sparrow, owls) to keep the row short; they could be added as "a review reports".

input.text: If you are an American alligator, the cone cells in your eyes hold four kinds of light-sensing pigment, where a human has three. One of them sits in a single cone and senses light most strongly at 535 nanometers. If you are a saltwater crocodile, your three kinds of single cone sense violet, green and red light most strongly.
input.note: Only one of the alligator's four pigment peaks is recorded (535 nm), so the others are left out. Caimans and most crocodiles are not covered by this row.

input.text: If you are a bold jumping spider, your front eyes scan in a different pattern depending on whether moving dots move like a living animal and whether the dots form a shape. If you are a gray wall jumping spider, small, fast, thin stripes weaken the response of your front eyes' retinas. Nobody has measured how most other jumping spiders see movement, and in the magnolia green jumping spider the side-eye retina is less refined for motion than in the other jumping spiders studied.
input.note: Left out the 120 to 1200 degrees/s turning speeds (R14) and the 16 degrees/s figure (R15) because those records name only the family, not a species.

input.text: A review reports two kinds of color-sensing cell in cattle, sheep, goats and horses, where a human has three, and you very likely have two as well. A blue-sensing cell has been measured in the white-tailed deer, and a green-sensing cell in the fallow deer.
input.note: R6 (white-tailed deer) only states cones and rods, not a cone count, so I did not cite it for "two"; I left out wavelength figures because they have no comparison job.

input.text: Ultraviolet is light a human cannot see at all, and in the blue tit, the European starling and the Eurasian blackbird a kind of color-sensing cell peaks in it, between 360 and 375 nanometers. A review reports that the blue tit's lens and cornea let ultraviolet through, passing half the light at 315 nanometers, so if you are a songbird you very likely sense ultraviolet too. If you are a mallard, that cell peaks at 415 nanometers, in violet, and if you are a cormorant you very likely get almost no ultraviolet, since the lens and cornea of the pied cormorant block it.
input.note: Left out the house sparrow's 445 nm cell (R13) because it is not the ultraviolet cell, so no record gives its ultraviolet peak. Left out the goldfinch's 399 nm (partial) and the great cormorant's 405 nm to keep the row short.

input.text: Nobody has measured how fast a flicker your eyes can follow if you are a gray squirrel, a fox squirrel or a Eurasian red squirrel. In relatives, a compilation reports that American red squirrels see flicker up to about 60 flashes a second, the same as a human, and golden-mantled ground squirrels see it above 100. The southern flying squirrel, which is active at night, cannot follow flicker above about 10 to 15 flashes a second.
input.note: No cff_hz record exists for Sciurus, so the row stays at i and lists measured relatives only.

input.text: If you are a red-winged blackbird, your two eyes together take in about 315 degrees, nearly a full circle, and they overlap over about 50 degrees in front of you. If you are a mallard, the overlap in front is about 20 degrees. For most other birds, including house sparrows and American robins, nobody has measured how wide you see.
input.note: Kept to species with measured records; other measured species (mallard total, goldfinch, grebe, anhinga) left out for length.

input.text: If you are a chicory, your flower heads open in the early morning and fade as daylight reaches its greatest intensity. A review reports that if you are a black locust, your leaflets move by day and by night, and they stand more erect in stronger light. For most plants, nobody has measured how you sense light or how you keep track of the time of day.
input.note: No record covers green light specifically, so the row does not mention green.

input.text: If you are an eastern gray squirrel, the one squirrel tested read about 4 cycles a degree on a grating test, about an eighth of the 30 a human reads, and fox squirrels tested at about 2. In the Eurasian red squirrel, a relative in your genus, the cone cells are densest in a horizontal streak, and you very likely have the same. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is or how much of it your two eyes share.
input.note: No record gives field of view or binocular overlap for any squirrel, so the row says so. The 4 cycles a degree is from a single eastern gray squirrel.

input.text: Birds differ widely in how sharply they see, and for most species nobody has measured it. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. If you are a house sparrow, you read about 5, and if you are a mallard, about 12, estimated from the density of cells in the retina. If you are a Eurasian magpie or a western jackdaw, a review reports about 30 from behavior tests, close to a human.
input.note: No record for spacing of light-sensing cells (interreceptor_deg), so it is left out; figures stay with the species named.

input.text: If you are a honeybee, a lamp that looks steady to a human can look like it is flashing to you, because you can see flicker up to about 200 flashes a second, where a human stops at about 60. If you are a bumblebee, you very likely see flicker up to about 130 flashes a second, since that is what was measured in a relative, Bombus hortorum. If you are any other kind of bee or a wasp, nobody has measured how fast you see.
input.note: Left out the photoreceptor speed records (R2, R3, R5): they give impulse-response half-widths, not a flicker limit, and R5 is a fly.

input.text: Nobody has measured whether a heron, egret or coot senses ultraviolet, the light just beyond violet. If you are a rock pigeon, your violet-sensing cells absorb most strongly at about 410 nanometers, and in a whooping crane the same kind of pigment, made in a laboratory, absorbs most at about 405. Nobody has measured how much ultraviolet passes through the front of the eye to those cells in any of these birds.
input.note: No record for herons, egrets or coots; peafowl and quail transmission figures left out because numbers do not travel to other genera.

input.text: Nobody has measured how fast a light can flicker before you stop seeing the flicker. A review reports that a rock pigeon still sees flicker at about 75 flashes a second and a chicken at about 85, where a human stops at about 60. Both are birds that walk and peck on the ground, and whether a wading bird sees flicker as quickly as they do is unknown.
input.note: No record covers herons, egrets, cranes or other waders; only rock pigeon (75 Hz) and chicken (87 Hz) are measured, both via a review (Boström 2016).

input.text: If you are a European rabbit, crouching in the freeze position gives you a field of view of 360 degrees, and only about 25 degrees of it, straight ahead, is seen by both eyes. You have round pupils and two kinds of color-sensing cell, blue and green, and you see about a tenth of the fine detail a human sees. A review reports that you have no tapetum, the reflective layer behind the retina, and these measurements come from the European rabbit alone, since none are recorded for cottontails, hares or pikas.
input.note: Left out R9 (Leporidae field) and the Iberian rabbit carry, since fields travel only within a genus; peak wavelengths dropped as they had no job.

input.text: If you are an American bullfrog, you start to dodge a looming object when it spans about 20 degrees of your vision, roughly ten human thumbs held at arm's length. If you are a European toad, nerve cells that pick out moving prey are masked when a textured background moves at the same speed as the prey, and if you are a cane toad, a review reports that you strike at a moving insect-like model. Nobody has measured how you see motion in most other frogs and toads, including the American toad.
input.note: Left out R3 (Japanese toad) and R5 (Guayaquil dwarf frog) to keep the row short; both could be added.

input.text: Look at your leaves, your stem and your flowers, and you will find no eye among them. Nobody has measured whether any part of you forms an image of what is around you.
input.note: R1 describes moth and beetle eyes, so I did not cite it. No record covers plant eyes, so the row rests on no record. Please check "no eye" against a plant source.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and every insect eye measured so far sees far less fine detail than that. If you are an orange sulphur you see about 0.7 cycles a degree, if you are an Old World swallowtail about 0.5 (a compilation reports this), and if you are a common green darner about 2. For most other insects, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out the facet-angle figures and the other measured species to keep the row short; no record states a mechanism sentence, so none is included.

input.text: Only a few jumping spiders have had the spacing of their light-sensing cells measured, and nobody has measured how sharply most of you see. In the big front eyes of Phidippus johnsoni, neighboring cells sit about 9 minutes of arc apart, where a degree has 60 minutes. In the side eyes of the bold jumping spider, the sharpest zone has cells about half a degree apart.
input.note: Left out the 3.8 cycles a degree (R3) because its quote gives only a visual angle, and left out the 0.4 to 2 degree review range (R5) to avoid decimals.

input.text: If you are a white-tailed deer, you see a fifth or less of the fine detail a human sees, and a light-reflecting layer called the tapetum lucidum covers the upper part of your eye and overlaps the strip where you see most sharply. A review reports the same layer in deer generally, so other deer very likely have it too. Nobody has measured how dim a light you can see by, and nobody has tested how you judge depth.
input.note: Dim-light sensitivity and depth cue have no deer records (only horse, sheep, cattle), so both are stated as unmeasured.

input.text: A compilation of measurements reports that a red-tailed hawk reads about 17 cycles a degree, roughly half of a human's 30, and that a black kite reads about 33, close to a human, while the eagle Aquila audax reads up to 138. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a bald eagle, an osprey or most other species in your group, and the measured ones differ too much for any figure to stand in for you.
input.note: Left out the 160 cycles a degree book figure (R13) because it names no species. Left out interreceptor_deg because no record has it.

input.text: If you are a bold jumping spider, each of the eyes beside your two big front eyes sees an area about 70 degrees wide and about 100 degrees tall, so it reaches farther up and down than side to side. For other jumping spiders, nobody has measured these fields. Nobody has measured how far all your eyes together see around you, or how much the fields of your two side eyes overlap.
input.note: Left out R8 (about 25 degrees of overlap, Blest 1981): it is a genus-level discussion statement and the row's binocular trait is unknown. Also left out the Phidippus johnsoni and Menemerus carried values, since they don't fit one plain sentence.

input.text: If you are a honeybee, you have a kind of color-sensing cell for ultraviolet, which is light that humans cannot see at all, and it senses light most strongly at about 345 nanometers. The same cell peaks at about 335 nanometers in the buff-tailed bumblebee and about 345 in the common eastern bumblebee. Nobody has measured how far into the ultraviolet your sensitivity reaches, so only the peak is known.
input.note: Left out wasps: the record for Dolichovespula norwegica (R14) lists only blue and green cells, so an ultraviolet claim would not fit every species here.

input.text: A human stops seeing a light as flickering at about 60 flashes a second, and the butterflies measured so far see flicker well beyond that. Danaus chrysippus, a close relative of the monarch, responds to flicker at 160 to 210 flashes a second, and the skipper Epargyreus clarus at 180 to 200. Nobody has measured how fast you see flicker if you are a ladybird beetle, a stink bug, a dragonfly, or one of most of the other butterflies.
input.note: Left out the drone fly corner frequency (R9) and the dragonfly ocellus value (R28): neither states how fast a compound eye follows flicker.

input.text: If you are a pond slider, you have four kinds of color-sensing cone, one of them for ultraviolet, and a review reports that you see about a fifth of the detail a human sees. Sharpness has also been measured in the green anole, the brown anole, the box turtle and the common watersnake, but in most lizards, snakes and turtles nobody has measured it. Nobody has measured how far around you can see, and the shape of your pupil is recorded for only a few species, such as the round pupils of the painted turtle and the garter snake.
input.note: No record gives field of view for any reptile, so the row says so. Ultraviolet sense is stated only for the pond slider.

input.text: Straight ahead, your two eyes look at the same patch of the world, and in the birds measured that patch is about 35 degrees wide in the red-tailed hawk, American kestrel and Cooper's hawk, 40 in the bald eagle, and 45 in the crested caracara. Behind your head the red-tailed hawk has a blind area of about 80 degrees and Cooper's hawk one of about 60. For most hawks, eagles and falcons, nobody has measured how wide the whole field is, and for many nobody has measured the overlap either.
input.note: Left out total field widths (278 and 300 degrees): their quotes give only the blind areas, not those values.

input.text: A review estimates that you take in about 240 degrees around you, where a human takes in 180, and that your two eyes overlap by 30 to 60 degrees. For dim light you have more rods than a human, even in the center of the retina where a human has none, and a mirror layer behind the retina called the tapetum, which was full-sized in 70 percent of 539 Swedish dogs and absent in about 2 percent. Nobody has measured how well you judge depth.
input.note: Depth sentence rests on no record (depth_cue unknown); R5 is a cat record on focusing range, so I left it out.

input.text: Jumping spiders have eight simple eyes, and you very likely have eight as well. If you are a bold jumping spider, your two big front eyes follow a moving target precisely only while the smaller eyes beside them guide them. Nobody has measured what each of your eyes does in most species, so for you the full division of work is unknown.
input.note: Left out Lyssomanes (vestigial rear median eyes, R5) and the Menemerus and Habronattus findings (R1, R3) because they belong to other genera and the row would grow past three sentences.

input.text: If you are a grey heron, a little egret or a tick bird, your head most often makes one bob for each step you take, and the same has been filmed in other herons and egrets. If you are a black-crowned night heron, you see about 320 degrees around you at once. Nobody has measured how your head and eyes move or how wide you see if you are a great blue heron, a great egret or a green heron.
input.note: Left out pigeon, moorhen and squacco numbers since the row speaks to the heron; Ardeidae field of 170 degrees (R30) is one eye only and was not needed.

input.text: Nobody has measured how wide you see, how sharply you see, how little light you need, or how you judge distance. Crocodilians have a reflecting layer in the eye for night vision, and in the saltwater crocodile it is brightest behind a furrowed slit, so you very likely have one as well. The only sharpness figure comes from the saltwater crocodile, about 9 cycles a degree against a human's 30, and in six crocodilian species the eyes were well focused in air for distant targets and severely defocused underwater.
input.note: No record measures the American alligator itself for any of these traits; the sharpness figure is kept with the saltwater crocodile, and R4 does not list which six species were tested.
